title: Issues: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge how issues are typed, handled formally or informally, decided by the right authority and escalated, and pick the reason that explains the verdict.
question: At Tarnside College, the contractor and the head of estates agree on site to add extra ductwork and start the same day, without checking the budget. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?

teach.body: When judging issue handling, ask four things. Is it really a project issue, and of the right type, rather than a risk or a matter for the business? Is it handled with the right formality: formal in the issue register, informal or sensitive in the daily log, trivial matters not swamping decisions? Is it decided by someone with the authority, within delegated limits and a change budget? And is it escalated properly: an issue report within tolerance, an exception report only for a forecast breach?

teach.h: The technique, with the judging question at each step

steps.label: Capture
steps.sub: Right type? Formal or informal? Registered?

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: Effect on targets, tolerances, business case, risks

steps.label: Implement
steps.sub: Corrective action; records and baseline updated

teach.caption: Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement (10.3.1). Assessment is best done cooperatively.

children.label: Exception report
children.sub: Board decides; may ask for an exception plan

rows.label: Used when
values: Stage or project tolerance forecast to break

teach.caption: Within tolerance means an issue report, not an exception report (10.5, 11.5).

teach.h: Delegating authority and the change budget
teach.body: The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications, but it may delegate approval to a change authority or the project manager. Delegation is about approving changes, not doing them: implementation still runs through the PM and work packages. Delegated authority should come with a change budget so approved changes can be funded, and both are reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change. A request for change should name the products affected and its justification.

head: What happens
Verdict and why
rows: Change agreed on site; work starts at once
Every minor query raised as a formal issue
Change authority given limits and a budget
Sensitive staffing matter kept in the daily log
Within-tolerance change sent as an exception
Event needing a business response logged as a project RFC

teach.h: Worked scenario: Tarnside Engineering Skills Centre
teach.body: Tarnside's last lessons report said changes were agreed on site without checking the budget. So in initiation, project manager Leah Whitfield's issue management approach makes the head of estates, Craig Dunmore, a change authority for changes up to £20,000, with a £100,000 change budget. In stage 3, the contractor proposes a cheaper mezzanine fixing: Leah captures it, assesses it with the cost consultant, and Craig approves it. A request for six more welding bays at £55,000 is beyond Craig's limit but within stage tolerance, so Leah writes an issue report for the board.

items: Ask whether it is an issue at all: already happened, relevant to the project, needing project management consideration.
Check formality and type: formal, informal or sensitive; request for change, off-specification, problem, concern.
Check authority: who may decide at this size, and is there a change budget?
Pick the reason that explains this verdict, not a true fact about issues in general.

teach.text: Traps: (1) a within-tolerance issue goes to the decision-maker in an issue report, never as an exception report; (2) the board can delegate approving changes, but the PM still implements them; (3) the risk budget funds risk responses, the change budget funds approved changes; (4) an event that needs a response from the business, not the project, is not a project issue.

items: Good handling follows capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement.
Formal issues in the issue register; informal or sensitive ones in the daily log; avoid swamping with trivia.
Board is ultimate authority; delegated change authority needs limits and a change budget.
Escalate beyond delegated limits; use an exception report only for a forecast tolerance breach.
Close issues once decided and implemented; business-level events are not project issues.

summary: You can now judge whether an issue is typed and handled with the right formality, decided by the right authority within a change budget and escalated in the right report. You can also choose the reason that genuinely explains the verdict in a 2 x 2 question.

A.q: Tarnside College's project is in its structural works stage. Greystack Build's site manager proposes using a different fixing method for the mezzanine to save a week. Project manager Leah Whitfield has captured the proposal as a request for change in the issue register. What should she do next?
options: Approve it, because it saves time in the stage plan
Raise an exception report to the board
Ask the contractor to start the new method
Assess its impact on targets and the business case
A.why: After capture, the issue is assessed: does it affect the project, and how, including targets and tolerances, the business case, other products and the risk profile (10.3.1).

whyNot.0: Approval comes after assessment and recommendation, and only from someone with the authority.
whyNot.1: Nothing suggests a forecast breach of stage tolerance, so there is no exception to report.
whyNot.2: Work on a change starts only after it has been assessed and approved.

A.q: Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline is in its foundations stage. The cloud provider unexpectedly offers the society a free analytics tool that could help member services produce reports, a benefit nobody had planned for. Which type of issue is this, and how should it be handled?
options: Business opportunity, to capture and assess
An opportunity risk, recorded in the risk register
Request for change, approved by the change authority
Off-specification, recorded as a concession
A.why: A business opportunity is an issue with unanticipated positive consequences for the project or user organization; it is captured and assessed like any issue (10.1).

whyNot.1: The offer has already been made, so it is an issue to consider, not an uncertain future event.
whyNot.2: No one is yet proposing a change to a baseline, and approval would follow assessment.
whyNot.3: An off-specification is a product failing its specification; nothing has failed here.

A.q: On Calderbrook's Permits Online project, the board has delegated authority to project manager Hannah Okoro to approve changes up to £10,000 each, with a change budget of £40,000. £35,000 has already been spent. A worthwhile request for change costing £8,000 arrives. What should Hannah do?
options: Approve it, as it is below her £10,000 limit
Reject it, as the change budget is nearly spent
Escalate it, as the budget left is too small
Approve it and raise an exception report
A.why: Delegated authority is limited by the change budget; with £5,000 left she cannot fund an £8,000 change, so the decision goes to the board (10.2.4, 10.2.5, 10.3.1).

whyNot.0: The per-change limit is met, but there is not enough change budget left to fund it.
whyNot.1: Rejecting a worthwhile change only for lack of her budget would bypass the board, which has the authority to decide.
whyNot.3: She cannot approve unfunded changes, and a change request is not by itself a forecast tolerance breach.

B.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in its development stage. The head of new product development asks for one more consumer panel round, costing £8,000 and one week. The board has not delegated change authority, and stage tolerances are plus or minus £25,000 and two weeks. Which report should the project manager use to take this to the board?
options: An exception report, as the change needs the board
An issue report, as it is within stage tolerance
A highlight report, as it can wait for the next one
An end stage report, as the stage plan changes
B.why: The change is within stage tolerance, so it needs an issue report setting out impact, options and a recommendation for the board, which holds change authority (10.5, 11.2.6).

whyNot.0: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance, which this is not.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports give periodic stage status; a request for change needs its own decision paper.
whyNot.3: The end stage report is produced at the stage boundary, not to seek a decision on one change.

B.q: Tarnside College's board has made the head of estates, Craig Dunmore, a change authority for changes up to £20,000. Craig has just approved a change to the fume extraction ducting. Which role should now issue the amended work package to the contractor's team manager?
options: Craig Dunmore, as the change authority
Project support, maintaining the register
The project manager, Leah Whitfield
The executive, as ultimately accountable
B.why: Delegated change authority is about approving changes, not implementing them; the project manager implements approved changes through work packages (10.2.4, table 10.2).

whyNot.0: Craig's delegated authority is to approve the change, not to direct the contractor's team.
whyNot.1: Project support updates the issue register but does not authorize work packages.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable for the project, but work packages are authorized by the project manager.

B.q: A resident emails Calderbrook's project team to say the online permit form crashes on older phones. Project manager Hannah Okoro decides it is a problem, rates its severity and priority using the agreed scales, and has it entered in the issue register. Which step of the issues technique has she just completed?
options: Capture
Assess
Recommend
Decide
B.why: Capturing an issue means determining its type, its initial severity and priority, and registering it (10.3.1).

whyNot.1: Assessing follows capture and looks at the effect on targets, tolerances, the business case and risks.
whyNot.2: Recommending identifies and evaluates options for whoever has the authority.
whyNot.3: Deciding is approving, rejecting or deferring by someone with authority, after a recommendation.

C.q: Tarnside College's project is in its structural works stage. Greystack's site manager and the head of estates agree on site to add extra ventilation ducts, and the work starts the same day. Nobody checks the budget or records the change. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because decisions should be made at the most local level
Yes, because the head of estates knows the building best
No, because every change must go to the project board
No, because it bypasses assessment and approval
C.why: Changes to the baseline must be captured, assessed and approved or rejected by someone with the authority before being implemented (10.2.3, 10.3.1).

whyNot.0: Decisions should be made locally where knowledge sits, but within delegated authority and change control.
whyNot.1: Expertise matters in assessment, but it does not replace change control.
whyNot.2: The board may delegate approval to a change authority or the PM, so not every change goes to the board.

C.q: During initiation of Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline, the board delegates authority to project manager Mairi Campbell to approve changes up to £25,000 each. It gives her no change budget, saying she should find savings elsewhere in the plan. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM should work within stage tolerance
Yes, because change authority is about approving changes
No, because the board cannot delegate change approval
No, because authority needs a budget to fund changes
C.why: Delegated authority should come with a change budget so that approved changes can actually be funded and implemented (10.2.5).

whyNot.0: The PM does work within tolerance, but tolerance is not a fund for approved changes.
whyNot.1: Delegation is about approving, but without a budget approved changes cannot be paid for.
whyNot.2: The board can delegate approval to a change authority or the PM.

C.q: Wenmoor Community Health's project is in its Eastfield pilot stage. The commissioner announces that it will re-tender all community nursing contracts in three years, after the project has closed; the announcement does not change the SPA's scope. Project manager Ellie Chandran logs it as a request for change and asks the board to change the project to prepare the trust's bid. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because any event affecting the trust is a project issue
Yes, because external events are a type of issue
No, because it needs a response from the business
No, because it is a risk, as the tender is years away
C.why: A project issue is an event relevant to the project needing project management consideration; this needs a response from the trust as a business, not a change to the project's baseline (10.1).

whyNot.0: Events matter to the project when they affect it; this one concerns the trust's future contracts.
whyNot.1: External events can be issues, but that does not explain why this one should change the project.
whyNot.3: The announcement has been made, and it does not threaten the project's objectives either.

reteach.title: Pocket money and the family rules
reteach.question: A teenager may spend up to £10 of a monthly allowance on things for a school trip; bigger costs go to the parents. How does that map to change control?

blocks.body: The family rules say who can approve what and how requests are made: the issue management approach. The parents are the ultimate authority, like the project board. The teenager's £10 limit is delegated change authority, and the allowance is the change budget: without it the limit is useless. A £40 request goes to the parents with a short note of options: the issue report. Spending without asking is like changes agreed on site.

blocks.text: Being allowed to approve is not the same as doing the work: after the parents agree, the teenager still has to arrange the purchase, just as the PM implements approved changes.

explain.body: Assessment of issues and options is best done cooperatively, drawing on team members and stakeholders, especially when impacts reach beyond the project.

test.q: On Calderbrook's project, a request arrives to add a Welsh language version of the online form. Project manager Hannah Okoro assesses it by asking Kestrel Lane's delivery manager, the contact centre manager and the ICT infrastructure manager for their input. How well does this apply the issues practice, and why?
options: Well, because assessing together is recommended
Well, because the PM has authority to approve it
Poorly, because assessment is the team manager's job
Poorly, because the board should do the assessment
test.why: Assessing issues and developing options is best approached cooperatively, using input from team members and stakeholders (10.3.1).

whyNot.1: Nothing says Hannah holds delegated authority, and approval is a separate step from assessment.
whyNot.2: The PM leads the assessment, drawing in team members and stakeholders; it is not the team manager's job.
whyNot.3: The PM assesses issues; the board decides on escalated ones.

explain.body: Whoever has authority may approve, reject, defer or ask for more information on a request for change; for an off-specification they may grant a concession. For an exception, the board may ask for an exception plan.

test.q: Fernhollow Kitchen's board reviews an issue report on adding a fifth consumer panel round. The cost estimate in the report is unclear, and the board cannot tell whether the change would affect the trials stage. Which decision is most appropriate?
options: Approve it and fix the cost later
Reject it until a new stage starts
Grant a concession for the extra round
Ask for more information first
test.why: Requesting more information is a valid decision when the board cannot yet judge the impact of a request for change (10.3.1, table 10.1).

whyNot.0: Approving without understanding the cost and impact undermines change control.
whyNot.1: Rejecting on timing alone does not address the unclear assessment.
whyNot.2: A concession applies to an off-specification, not a request for change.

explain.body: Judgement is needed on what to record formally. Too many trivial issues swamp the decision-makers; minor matters can be handled informally.

test.q: On Carrowford's half marathon project, project manager Kezia Oduya records every volunteer's question about T-shirt sizes as a formal issue, each with its own issue report to the board. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because every question is an issue to record
Yes, because issue reports keep the board informed
No, because trivial matters swamp the decisions
No, because volunteers are not project stakeholders
test.why: Judgement is needed on what to record and escalate; too many trivial issues swamp decision-making (10.2.2).

whyNot.0: Minor matters can be handled informally rather than formally registered.
whyNot.1: The board is informed through highlight reports, not an issue report for every small query.
whyNot.3: Volunteers are stakeholders; the problem is the formality, not who raised it.

explain.body: Delegated change authority and the change budget are reviewed at each stage boundary, or when tolerances change, so they stay right for the next stage.

test.q: At the end of Tarnside College's design and procurement stage, the project board reviews the change authority's limits and the change budget before construction begins, and raises both. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the board must approve each change
Yes, because limits are reviewed at boundaries
No, because delegation is set once in initiation
No, because the change budget belongs to the PM
test.why: Delegated change authority and the change budget are reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change (10.2.4).

whyNot.0: The board can delegate approval, so it need not approve each change itself.
whyNot.2: Delegation can be revisited at stage boundaries as the project's needs change.
whyNot.3: The board allocates the change budget along with delegated authority.
